For nine days, one email sat in my drafts. I'm Jomon, and I'd made a mistake in the quarterly figures I sent to our biggest client. A small one, a wrong column, but they'd already shared it with their board.
The email was four sentences long. I'd written it on day one. “I found an error in the figures I sent. Here is the corrected sheet. I'm sorry for the confusion. Happy to explain on a call.”
Every morning I opened it, felt my stomach drop, imagined the reply, and closed it. I cleaned my desk. I answered twenty other emails. My friend Jyoti asked why I looked so tense.
On day nine, Jyoti sat next to me and said, “Send it while I watch.”
I did. The client replied in an hour: “Thanks for flagging. Appreciate it.”
Nine days of dread for one hour of waiting.

qa.a: The email sat in the drafts for nine days.

qa.a: Jomon felt dread imagining the client's reply, so the small task carried a feeling far larger than itself.

Research mentor's note, doctoral cohort, March.
Sabina, a first-year PhD student, told me today that she has not replied to her supervisor, Dr Shalini Rao, in eleven days. The email asked a simple question: whether Sabina could share her draft chapter by the end of the month.
Sabina said she had written the reply several times. Each time, she imagined Dr Rao reading the draft and being disappointed, and she closed the window. She has been working on the chapter at night while avoiding the inbox by day.
She looked exhausted and ashamed. She kept saying, “It's just one email. Why can't I do it?”
I pointed out that the email itself is small; the fear attached to it is big.
What I did next: we wrote a two-line reply together in my office, “Yes, I'll share it on the 28th. It's rough, and I'd value your comments.” She sent it before leaving. I will check in with her on the 29th.

The email to Francis is still in drafts. Day six.
He was my team lead before he left, and I'd promised him the handover notes by the 10th. It's the 22nd. The notes are done. They've been done since the 15th. I just have to attach them and say sorry for the delay.

It's two lines and an attachment. Two lines.
Tomorrow: 9 a.m., before I check anything else. I've written it on my hand in pen: FRANCIS 9AM. If I don't send it by 9:05, I'll ask Mehul at the next desk to watch me press send.
— Arnab

passage:
Pooja had been avoiding her tax-filing paperwork for three weeks. Every evening in her Mumbai flat she'd look at the folder, feel a hot wave of guilt, call herself useless, and turn on the TV.
Her friend Kavitha, visiting, watched this happen twice. The second time, she said, “What if, instead of shouting at yourself, you just said, ‘Okay, I delayed. That's human.’ And then did five minutes?”
Pooja laughed bitterly. “Five minutes won't finish it.”
“It's not supposed to. It's supposed to start.”
That evening, Pooja said the sentence out loud, feeling silly. Then she set a timer for five minutes and opened the folder. She found the first form. Filled in her name, address, PAN.
The timer rang. She kept going for another half hour. The guilt was still there, but quieter.

qa.a: Kavitha sees it as normal and human, and seems patient and caring rather than judging.

“I'm supposed to be writing the grant report. It was due last Friday. I'm the worst.”
“You're not the worst.”
“I am, Disha. I keep telling myself how lazy I am, and then I feel so bad I can't even open the file.”
“Does telling yourself you're lazy ever help you start?”
Ganga paused. “No. It makes me want to hide.”
“Okay. So try something else. Say, ‘I'm late, and that's okay, I'm going to do five minutes.’ Just five.”
“That sounds like a greeting card.”
“Humour me.”
Ganga sighed, then said it, half-mocking. She opened the file. Typed the heading. Then the first paragraph.
When Disha came back with tea twenty minutes later, Ganga was still typing. “Don't talk to me,” Ganga said, smiling. “I'm on a roll.”

For most of my twenties I believed the harsher I was with myself, the more I'd get done. I'm Ramesh. When I delayed something, I'd lie awake calling myself pathetic.
It didn't work. The more I shouted inside, the less I did.
Last year, my colleague Tushar noticed I'd been sitting on the audit summary for two weeks. He didn't scold. He said, “You're behind. Everyone gets behind. What's the smallest thing you could do in five minutes?”
I said, “Open the file and write the headings.”
“Do that. Then decide.”
It felt too gentle to work. But I did it. Five minutes became forty. The next day was easier.
Now, when I delay, I try to say, quietly, “Okay. You're human. Five minutes.” The guilt still comes. It just doesn't get to drive.

Dear Pankaj Bhaiya,

Remember you told me to watch when I pick up my phone? I tried it for three days. I'm a bit shocked.

I reach for it the second anything goes quiet. Waiting for the bus. When the teacher is writing on the board. When the kettle is boiling. Even in the ad break of a show I'm already watching on a screen!

I don't decide to. My hand is already scrolling before I think. And the funny thing is, what I find isn't even good. Just new. A meme, a video, a friend's photo. Tiny bit of excitement, then gone.

I counted on Tuesday: 64 times.

I think it's a loop. Bored, grab, something new, repeat. I don't know how to break it yet, but at least now I can see it.

Naveen

I'm Aditi. Last month, Ma'am made us do this exercise: every time you pick up your phone, put a tick on your hand. By lunchtime, my hand was covered. I'd picked it up at every tiny gap. Walking between classes. Waiting for the photocopy. While my friend was talking, even.

It's like my brain learned: bored equals phone. It doesn't ask me first.

Then I just watched him for a week, without saying anything. Every day it was the same: he'd walk in from school, drop his bag, sink onto the sofa, and in the same second the phone was in his hand. Two hours gone. The sofa was the trigger.
So I stopped nagging and changed the room. We moved the charger to the kitchen. I put a bowl of fruit and his sketchbook on the dining table, where the light is good. He sits there now for the first half hour, eating and drawing.
He still uses his phone. But it isn't the first thing anymore. I felt so silly for nagging all that time, when the sofa was doing half the work.

Every day at 3:40, the school bus drops Ramesh at the gate. By 3:45 he's on the sofa with the phone. Not deciding. Just there, like a key turning a lock. By six, homework is untouched and he looks dull and cranky.

His hostel friend Amandeep suggested a different approach. “Put your shoes and socks by the bed tonight. Your jacket on the chair. And don't plan a big run. Ten minutes.”
“Ten minutes is nothing.”
“That's the point.”
That night, Divyansh laid out everything. At 6:30 the alarm rang. It was bitterly cold. But the socks were right there. He pulled them on, grumbling, then the shoes. He ran for ten minutes, breath steaming.
By the end of January, he was running twenty-five minutes, five days a week. The shoes still went by the bed every night.

Her flatmate Vandana, who ran every morning, asked what stopped her.
“I don't know. I think of running forty minutes, and I feel tired before I start.”
“Who said forty?”
“Isn't that what people do?”
Vandana laughed. “Start with ten. And take the shoes out of the box tonight.”
That night Ritu put the shoes and a T-shirt beside her bed in their Hyderabad flat. The next morning she saw them before she saw her phone. She pulled them on and went around the colony park twice. Ten minutes exactly.
She came home red-faced and oddly proud. For the next three weeks, the shoes lived by the bed, and she didn't miss a single weekday.

“Nandini, you're running now?”
“Trying, Ujjwal. Day twelve.”
“You? You said running was torture.”
“It is. That's why I cheat.”
“Cheat how?”
“Two things. One: every night I put my shoes right next to the bed, with socks inside them. So in the morning I step into them before my brain can argue.”
“And two?”
“Ten minutes. That's all I ask myself. If I want to stop at ten, I stop.”
“Do you stop?”
“Some days. Most days I do fifteen or twenty, because I'm already out.”
“Ten sounds too easy.”
“It's supposed to be easy. Last year I tried an hour a day and quit in a week.”
Ujjwal thought about it. “Can I join you? Tomorrow?”
“Shoes by the bed tonight,” Nandini said. “Socks inside.”

qa.a: Nandini is on day twelve.

passage:
The nurses' station at the city hospital was busy even at 3 p.m. Sunaina, twenty-five, had a pattern: every time a difficult relative left the desk, she grabbed her phone and scrolled. Five minutes, sometimes fifteen. Afterward she felt more drained, not less.
Her colleague Pradeep suggested, “Don't just stop. Replace it. When you feel that rush, walk to the end of the corridor and back. Or do the four-count breathing at the window.”
So she tried. Same trigger: a tense conversation. New action: a walk to the corridor window, four slow breaths. On a scrap of paper in her pocket she tallied how she felt after, on a scale from one to five.
After two weeks, the tally was mostly fours. The scrolling sheet from the week before had been mostly twos.
The stress still came. But the walk met the need.

qa.q: What did Sunaina tally on the scrap of paper?
qa.a: How she felt after each walk, on a scale from one to five.

qa.q: Why did Sunaina reach for the phone after difficult conversations?
qa.a: She felt stressed and wanted quick relief, even though scrolling left her more drained.

qa.q: Why did replacing the scrolling work better than simply stopping?
qa.a: The same cue now led to a walk and breathing that met her need for relief, and tracking showed it helped.

qa.q: How might Pradeep feel seeing Sunaina's tally of mostly fours?
qa.a: Pradeep would probably feel glad and a little proud that the suggestion helped.

grounding: The passage shows an adult keeping the stress cue but swapping scrolling for a short walk and breathing, and tracking the result.

passage:
Dear Jasleen,

You asked how I stopped doom-scrolling at work. I didn't stop, exactly. I swapped.

For months, every time my manager sent a tense message, I'd open my phone and scroll news for twenty minutes. I felt worse afterwards, but I kept doing it. It was the only break I gave myself.

So I kept the trigger and changed the action. Tense message arrives → I stand up, walk to the stairwell, go down one floor and back up. Then three slow breaths at the window.

I kept a small tally on a sticky note: how stressed before, how stressed after. The walk won almost every time.

It isn't magic. But I still get my break, just a better one.

Love,
Rashmi

qa.q: Where does Rashmi walk after a tense message?
qa.a: Rashmi walks to the stairwell, down one floor and back up.

qa.q: How did Rashmi feel after scrolling news for twenty minutes?
qa.a: Rashmi felt drained and worse afterward, yet kept doing it because it was the only break.

qa.q: Why did swapping the action work for Rashmi?
qa.a: It kept the same trigger and still gave a break, meeting the need for relief, while the tally showed it helped more.

qa.q: How might Jasleen react to Rashmi's method?
qa.a: Jasleen might feel encouraged and curious to try a similar swap.

grounding: The letter shows an adult keeping the stress trigger but replacing scrolling with a short walk and breathing, and tracking the result.

passage:
You asked how I got my screen time down, Manjula. I'll be honest: I didn't just delete the apps. I tried that. It lasted two days.
I'm Divyansh. I scroll when I'm stressed. Client yells, I scroll. Deadline moves, I scroll. It gives me a break, sort of. Then I feel worse.
What worked was keeping the same moment, the stress, and giving myself something else. A short walk around the office block. Or box breathing at my desk, four counts in, four hold, four out.
And I tracked it. Just a line in my notes app: stress before, stress after, what I did. After three weeks it was obvious. Walks helped. Scrolling didn't.
The need didn't go away. I still need a break when I'm stressed. I just stopped giving myself the one that didn't work.

qa.q: How long did deleting the apps last for Divyansh?
qa.a: It lasted two days.

qa.q: How does Divyansh feel after stress scrolling?
qa.a: Divyansh feels a brief break, then worse than before.

qa.q: Why did replacing scrolling with a walk or breathing work where deleting apps failed?
qa.a: It kept the same stress cue and still met the need for a break, and tracking showed which option helped.

qa.q: How might Manjula feel hearing this?
qa.a: Manjula might feel reassured that it doesn't take pure willpower, and curious to try a swap.

grounding: The monologue shows an adult keeping the stress cue but swapping scrolling for a walk or breathing, and tracking the effect.

In the foggy winter holidays, the village TV had broken. Imran, five, sat outside Nitin Chacha's shop.
“I'm bored,” he said. “Can I have your phone?”
“No,” said Chacha, weighing rice.
Imran kicked the step and groaned.
Chacha pushed an empty matchbox, some string and a few marigold petals across the counter.
Imran scowled. Then he tied the string to the matchbox. It became a cart. The petals became passengers.
By closing time, the cart had travelled to the well and back, and Imran had forgotten the phone.

qa.q: What did Nitin Chacha give Imran?
qa.a: An empty matchbox, some string and a few marigold petals.

qa.q: How did Imran feel before he started playing?
qa.a: He felt bored and restless, kicking the step, sighing and groaning.

qa.q: What did Chacha do that helped Imran's boredom turn into play?
qa.a: He said no to the phone, gave simple materials and let Imran have time without filling it for him.

qa.q: How might Chacha feel watching the matchbox cart travel?
qa.a: Chacha probably feels amused and quietly pleased that the boredom became imagination.

grounding: The passage shows a young child bored in winter holidays wanting a screen, and simple materials and time turning boredom into imaginative play.

Snow had closed Ankara's schools again. Selin, five, had played with every toy. After ten minutes at the window, she came to her father.
“Baba, I'm bored. Can I watch cartoons?”
Bilal, working at the kitchen table, said, “Not now. Here,” and handed her an empty grocery box and a marker.

“What is it?” he asked.
“A bakery,” she said. “You have to knock.”

The monsoon kept the Pune day care indoors all week. Yash, four, stood by the window after ten minutes of blocks. “Karthik Sir, I'm bored. Can we watch the tablet?”
“Not today,” said Karthik Sir. He put a tray on the floor: bottle caps, pegs, a scarf, some paper cups.
Yash frowned. “This is boring stuff.”
“Maybe,” said Sir, and went to help another child.
Yash pouted. He poked a cap. He stacked two cups and draped the scarf over them.
Soon the cups were a mountain, the pegs were climbers and the caps were snowballs. Yash was narrating an avalanche.

Vasudha, your teacher says you just stare out of the window in maths. Let me, your Simran Nani, tell you a story before you decide you're lazy.
When I was fourteen, in Amritsar, I was hopeless at English grammar. The teacher raced through tenses as if we'd all been born knowing them. I got lost in the first five minutes. After that, what was the point of listening? I drew birds in my margin all period.
Everyone called me dreamy. Lazy.
Then our old teacher retired and a new one came. She sat with me for ten minutes, went back to the basics I'd missed, and gave me work that was hard but not impossible.
Suddenly I was listening. I stopped drawing birds, well, mostly.
I wasn't lazy. The lessons just weren't where I was.

qa.q: What did young Simran draw in her margins?
qa.a: She drew birds in her margin all period.

qa.q: Why did young Simran stop listening in grammar class?
qa.a: She felt lost and discouraged after the first five minutes, since the lessons were far beyond her, so drawing felt easier than listening.

qa.q: At what point in the story did young Simran start listening?
qa.a: When the new teacher went back to the basics and gave work that was hard but not impossible.

qa.q: How might the new teacher have seen young Simran?
qa.a: The new teacher probably saw a student who was lost rather than lazy, and felt it was worth helping her catch up.

grounding: The grandmother's memory shows a teenager doodling in a class far beyond her, where boredom signalled a mismatch rather than laziness.

The fans in Class 9B had stopped working, and it was forty degrees outside. Asif sat by the window, sweating, while Sunaina Ma'am explained simple equations for the third day in a row.
Asif had learned them in Class 7 from his older cousin's books. He'd finished the worksheet in four minutes. Now he was drawing a detailed cricket stadium in the back of his notebook, then staring at the crows on the wall.
“Asif! Pay attention.”
“Sorry, Ma'am.”
But after class, Sunaina Ma'am picked up his worksheet and saw it was all correct, done in pencil in the margin before she'd even finished explaining. She looked at the stadium drawing, then at him.
“You're not being lazy, are you? You're bored because this is too easy.”
Asif nodded slowly, surprised. The next day she gave him a sheet of harder problems.

qa.q: How long did Asif take to finish the worksheet?
qa.a: He finished it in four minutes.

qa.q: How did Asif feel when Ma'am said he was bored because it was too easy?
qa.a: He felt surprised and relieved, since she understood he wasn't being lazy.

qa.q: Which of Sunaina Ma'am's actions helped Asif?
qa.a: She checked his worksheet, saw the real reason for his boredom and gave him harder problems the next day.

qa.q: How might Sunaina Ma'am have first seen Asif by the window?
qa.a: At first she probably saw a daydreaming, inattentive student, until the worksheet showed a mismatch.

grounding: The passage shows a teenager doodling in a hot class because the lesson is far below his level, and a teacher seeing a mismatch rather than laziness.

Leela, fifteen, sat in the physics tuition in Thrissur, drawing spirals down the edge of her notebook. The tutor had jumped from Newton's laws straight into problems about pulleys and inclined planes. Everyone else seemed to follow. Leela had understood nothing since the second slide.
Her friend Hafsa nudged her. “Aren't you listening?”
“There's no point,” Leela whispered. “I don't know what any of it means.” She looked out at the rain on the coconut trees.
After class, the tutor stopped her. “You were far away today. Are you just not interested?”
Leela shrugged, embarrassed. Then Hafsa said, “She's lost, Sir. From the start.”
The tutor paused. “Ah. Then boredom isn't the problem. The gap is.” He gave her a short sheet of basic force questions to try first.
